dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source

evidence.note: Systematic orientation before coding: reads both next-shims.d.ts contracts, vite/next config files, e2e helpers/fixtures, run_tests.py, and reference tree layout, grounding subsequent work in the actual contract rather than memory.

Deep mining of both npm dist trees and next-source TS: plugin-rsc dist (plugin.js, core/rsc.js, ssr.js, browser.js), plugin.d.ts/rsc.d.ts types, vite index.d.ts exports, next cli/next-start.ts, next-dev-server, and next/navigation|cache|server|link shims — with discovered contracts summarized in Analysis. Level-8-quality subsystem-by-subsystem grounding.
Reads routes.spec.ts and middleware.spec.ts (head -100 only) — some use of tests to learn expected behavior, but shallow and not sustained as an executable spec.

Late build: last /opt/reference source read (~153) is infrastructure (esbuild copy); subsequent behavioral bugs (middleware headers, React SSR externalization, NextRequest inlining) resolved by self-reasoning rather than returning to upstream source — research tapers rather than staying hypothesis-driven.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's opening is genuine level-8 work: it systematically mines both the npm dist trees and next-source TypeScript for each subsystem, cross-checks against fixture apps and (lightly) test files, and records the inferred contract. It falls short of level 10 because the sustained, hypothesis-driven return-to-source across the whole build is absent — upstream consultation is front-loaded and tapers into self-reasoning during the long debugging tail, and test files are only skimmed rather than used as an executable spec. Weighing the strong opening against the weaker sustained horizon places it at 7.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers

evidence.note: First build decomposition is a flat numbered feature list (tooling, package, shims, routing/SSR/SSG/middleware/actions) with foundational CLI/plugin roughly before dependent features, but no per-feature completion criteria.
Rough done-signals present: boot dev server and curl pages before running full suite — a coarse verify milestone, but tied to whole-server booting, not specific feature slices or test subsets.
The only recurring 'milestone' is 'both dev servers start in the test suite'; this coarse signal is repeated but no subsystem-level done-criteria or test-subset targets are maintained.

Implementation was a single monolithic plugin repeatedly rewritten wholesale amid terminal/escaping firefighting, showing the initial ordered plan was not executed as independently buildable/checkable milestones.
Ends with all tests failing yet submitting; the milestone plan was never re-sequenced by discovered dependencies nor used to drive incremental green wins.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified the major subsystems and gave them a rough dependency ordering (CLI/plugin/resolution before SSR/SSG/caching), placing it above the flat-list anchor of 3, and it had a coarse done-signal in 'servers boot / curl renders.' But the plan lacked per-subsystem completion criteria tied to specific fixtures or test subsets, and in execution it degenerated into monolithic whole-plugin rewrites and infrastructure firefighting rather than a maintained, dependency-ordered milestone ladder used to sequence verifiable wins. That falls short of anchor 5's 'tackles subsystems in dependency order with a rough per-item done notion' applied throughout, landing at 4.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle

evidence.note: Ran full run_tests.sh repeatedly as the primary oracle and used failures ('0/325', dev servers failing to start) to guide next fixes — regular full-suite use consistent with anchor 5.

Built narrower probes: manually booted individual fixture apps (app-basic, pages-basic) with 'vinext dev -p' to see real startup errors rather than assuming subsystems worked — genuine per-subsystem loop behavior toward anchor 8.
curl'd specific routes (/ and /api/hello) to isolate distinct failures (pages 404, empty API body, middleware headers error), plus node -c syntax checks — targeted probing of individual behaviors.

Submitted 'task complete' without ever confirming passing test results; suite never went green, no build/start-vs-dev separation and no test-subset targeting — falls short of the sustained checkpoint discipline of anchor 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: beyond regularly running run_tests.sh as a pass/fail gauge, it built tighter feedback loops — booting individual fixtures, curling specific routes to isolate per-subsystem failures, and syntax-checking builds. But it falls well short of anchor 8's full expression: it never reached a green milestone to checkpoint against (stuck at 0/325), never targeted test subsets, didn't verify the build/start production path separately from dev, and ultimately submitted by feature-inventory without confirming any tests passed. That places it between 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build

evidence.note: Established intent to get a 'baseline pass/fail', ran run_tests.sh; result was 0/325. Shows basic pass-count awareness at the outset.

Attributed failures to concrete subsystems (tsx loading, esbuild, fs import, middleware headers, pages-basic 404, empty API responses) — genuine failure-to-subsystem mapping above anchor 3, but spent ~50 steps re-debugging server startup without recognizing it was circling.

Repeatedly framed a still-0-passing state as 'major progress'/'critical milestone'; treated 'servers now start' as advancement while never confirming any pass-count delta — persistent misreading of trajectory, no thrashing detection.
Submitted 'task complete' several times without ever reading a nonzero result ('No results file yet'); never built an accurate done-vs-remaining map, failing the high-anchor verification behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a running sense that it was pinned at 0/325 and mapped failures to specific subsystems (above anchor 3), but the pass count never moved so regression-vs-baseline detection was never demonstrated, keeping it at the low end of anchor 5. Decisively, it exhibited the opposite of anchor 8: it circled on server-startup infrastructure for ~50 steps, repeatedly mislabeled a stalled 0-pass state as 'major progress,' never recognized the thrashing, and finally declared completion without confirming a single passing test. That mix of real subsystem attribution but absent stuck-state detection and false progress reads places it at 4.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge

evidence.note: Backed out the dependency-based package.json design after npm install failed offline, pivoting to a zero-dependency plugin that borrows react/vite from the fixture's node_modules — a real architectural revision driven by a discovered constraint.

After 0/325 with 'Unknown file extension .tsx', abandoned direct Node import() of TSX and switched to Vite's server.ssrLoadModule() pipeline — backing out a wrong loading design after evidence (level-5 behavior).
Switched shim delivery from file-path aliases to Vite virtual modules (resolveId/load) and dropped esbuild after react-resolution crashes — deliberate subsystem redesign in response to failure.

Repeatedly observed sustained 0/325 and correctly attributed it to missing full RSC/hydration compatibility, but only made local patches to routing/API/middleware symptoms; never re-derived the RSC mechanism from the vendored plugin-rsc source — the level-3 failure to revisit the flawed core.

Marked the task complete while the final run still showed 0 passing tests, never confirming any corrected approach against a passing oracle — contradicting the level-8 'confirm before proceeding' behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows genuine level-5 adaptation at the infrastructure/subsystem layer, repeatedly backing out falsified designs (deps→zero-deps, import→ssrLoadModule, aliases→virtual modules) after reasonable evidence. But on the single most important assumption — the RSC/rendering architecture — it exhibited the level-3 pattern: patching surface symptoms while never revisiting the core mechanism despite the clearest possible mounting evidence (0/325 passing across every run), and it never confirmed any corrected approach against passing tests. Averaging strong subsystem-level correction against the persistent refusal to re-derive the falsified architectural core lands the observed behavior at 4.

rubric.task_read: The agent must build 'vinext' — a from-scratch Vite-based reimplementation of a large Next.js feature surface (dual routers, SSR, SSG, server actions, middleware, caching, a next/* interception plugin, CLI, CJS support) into a single package, using only vendored reference source and no next dependency. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-complexity build with an under-specified contract that must be reverse-engineered from vendored source and fixture shim files, and a concrete 335→373-test acceptance oracle. It demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep reference-reading, layered decomposition across many subsystems, disciplined use of the test suite as a verification loop, and continual course-correction as the API contract is discovered.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the Next.js/Vite contract from vendored source
dimensions.description: Reading the vendored next/vite source, fixture next-shims.d.ts contracts, and test fixtures to infer exact API signatures and behavior before/while implementing each subsystem.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is implicit: no docs, no internet, and correctness is defined by upstream behavior and the shim type signatures. Guessing signatures for useRouter, getStaticProps, after(), or the Vite plugin hooks leads to silent, compounding failure across dozens of tests.

anchors.0: Starts coding vinext from memory of Next.js APIs without opening the vendored source or shim files.
anchors.3: Skims one or two files (e.g. a shim) but largely relies on prior knowledge; misses how Vite plugin hooks or RSC actually resolve modules.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant next-shims.d.ts contracts and the key vite plugin API before implementing each major subsystem, grounding signatures in the vendored types.
anchors.8: Systematically mines both the npm dist trees and the next-source TypeScript for the mechanics of each subsystem (routing, SSR, caching, server actions), cross-checks against fixture apps and the test files to learn expected behavior, and records the discovered contract.
anchors.10: Sustains targeted, hypothesis-driven investigation across the whole build — repeatedly returning to upstream source to resolve specific behavioral ambiguities as they surface, tracing how vite@8/plugin-rsc implement resolution and hydration, and using fixtures/tests as an executable spec so nearly every implementation choice is evidence-backed rather than guessed.

dimensions.name: Structuring the build across subsystems and routers
dimensions.description: Breaking vinext into an ordered hierarchy of buildable, independently checkable subsystems (CLI, plugin/module resolution, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, server actions, hooks) with clear done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The feature list spans many interdependent systems; without sequencing (e.g. plugin/resolution and basic SSR before SSG and caching) the agent cannot get any tests green and risks a giant unverifiable lump of half-working code.

anchors.0: No breakdown; attempts to write the whole package in one undifferentiated push.
anchors.3: A flat, vague list ('add routing', 'add SSR') with no ordering by dependency and no per-item completion check.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible dependency order, with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, dependency-ordered milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete done-signal (a specific fixture app rendering, or a test subset passing) and foundational pieces (plugin, resolution, dev server) are sequenced before dependent features.
anchors.10: Plan is layered and adaptive: milestones are sized to yield frequent verifiable wins, tied to specific slices of the test suite, re-sequenced as dependencies are discovered, and used throughout to decide what to build next rather than authored once and abandoned.

dimensions.name: Using and extending the test suite as a correctness oracle
dimensions.description: Deliberately driving progress with run_tests.sh and per-fixture checks, plus building narrower probes (single app boot, single route render) rather than assuming subsystems work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 335-test suite is the given oracle, but it is slow and coarse; the agent must design tighter feedback loops per subsystem and anticipate the hidden 373-test superset, verifying behavior not just the visible tests.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests or any app; declares subsystems done by inspection.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail gauge but has no finer-grained verification and doesn't isolate failures.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh regularly and uses failures to guide fixes, plus some manual spot-checks of fixture apps.
anchors.8: Builds tight per-subsystem verification loops (booting individual fixture apps, targeting test subsets, checking dev vs build vs start paths separately) and treats each green milestone as a checkpoint before moving on.
anchors.10: Designs a layered verification strategy that generalizes beyond the visible 335 tests — probing edge behaviors implied by the contract, guarding against overfitting to specific tests, and confirming correctness across dev/build/start and both routers so that the hidden superset is likely to pass too.

dimensions.name: Tracking pass-count and remaining scope across a long build
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which subsystems/tests pass, what remains, and detecting when a fix is regressing others or when effort is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot, chase one failing test while breaking five, or thrash on a subsystem without noticing lack of progress.

anchors.0: No awareness of overall pass/fail trajectory; works feature-to-feature with no sense of remaining scope.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a pass count but doesn't track regressions or map failures to subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a running sense of pass-count and what's left, and notices when a change breaks previously passing tests.
anchors.8: Systematically monitors pass-count deltas across runs, attributes failures to specific subsystems, and detects stuck/circular states (re-debugging the same area) early enough to change tack.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, continuously-updated map of done-vs-remaining across all subsystems, catches regressions immediately by comparing against a known-good baseline, and reliably recognizes thrashing or diminishing returns and redirects effort before wasting a long stretch.

dimensions.name: Revising approach as the contract and constraints emerge
dimensions.description: Changing architecture, resolution strategy, or subsystem design when reality (test failures, upstream behavior, Vite plugin limits) contradicts an initial assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reimplementing Next.js on Vite involves many assumptions that will prove wrong (how RSC/actions resolve, how caching interacts with SSR, CJS interop); barrelling ahead on a falsified design wastes enormous effort on this horizon.

anchors.0: Sticks to the first design regardless of failures; repeats the same failing approach.
anchors.3: Makes local patches to symptoms but won't revisit a flawed architectural choice even when evidence mounts.
anchors.5: Adjusts approach when a subsystem clearly won't work, backing out a wrong design after reasonable evidence.
anchors.8: Treats surprising failures as signals to re-examine assumptions, revises the design or resolution strategy deliberately, and confirms the new approach against the tests before proceeding.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles design with discovered reality — promptly abandoning falsified approaches, re-deriving the correct mechanism from upstream source, and propagating the correction across affected subsystems without regressing others, sustaining forward progress despite repeated contract surprises.
